Which definition correctly describes oscillatory motion?
Periodic motion along the same path on either side of equilibrium
Any motion that repeats with time
Motion on a circle at constant speed
Oscillatory motion follows the same path to either side of equilibrium, between two turning points.
A system completes N = 20 oscillations in Δt = 8 s. What are its period and frequency?
The correct relation between frequency and period is:
ν = N/Δt and T = Δt/N imply νT = 1. Angular frequency is ω = 2πν.
The amplitude of an oscillation is:
The maximum displacement magnitude: distance from equilibrium to a turning point
The distance travelled in a complete oscillation
A = |x_max| is a nonnegative scalar. The distance between turning points is 2A.
A spring oscillator in water has b = 0.5 s⁻¹ and T′ = 2 s. After how many periods does its amplitude halve?
D = bT′ = 1 and N½ = ln(2)/D ≈ 0.7: amplitude halves before the first period has finished.
For damping coefficient b = 0.25 s⁻¹, the amplitude decay time τ is:
τ = 1/b = 4 s. At this time A(τ) = A₀/e.
Within the oscillatory regime, increasing the viscosity of the medium makes the amplitude decay time:
Decrease, because b increases and τ = 1/b
Increase, because the pendulum oscillates more slowly
Greater viscosity increases resistance and b, reducing τ = 1/b. Critically damped and overdamped returns do not produce repeated oscillations.
A linear harmonic oscillator is acted on by the force:
The elastic restoring force is proportional and opposite to displacement. F = −r·v describes resistance, not the restoring force.
In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is:
a = −(k/m)y = −ω²y. Its magnitude is greatest at turning points and zero at equilibrium.
A gravitational pendulum approximately undergoes harmonic motion only when:
The angle is small (θ < 6°), allowing sin θ ≈ θ
F = −mg sin θ is not linear in θ. For small angles the approximation is valid: the error is about 0.17% at 5.7°, and k = mg/L.
The small-angle pendulum period T = 2π√(L/g) does NOT depend on:
The period depends only on L and g. Approximate amplitude independence allows pendulums to measure time.
For a spring oscillator with k = 50 N/m and m = 2 kg, the period is:
The velocity of a harmonic oscillator leads displacement by:
v = Aω cos(ωt + φ₀) = Aω sin(ωt + φ₀ + π/2). Acceleration differs from displacement by π.
For m = 200 g, F_max = 200 N and E = 40 J, amplitude and angular frequency are:
A = 2E/F = 0.4 m; k = F/A = 500 N/m; ω = √(k/m) = 50 rad/s. Thus y(t) = 0.4 sin(50t) m.
At what displacement are kinetic and potential energies equal, for A = 14.14 cm?
Ec = Ep and E = ½kA² imply ½ky² = ¼kA², giving y = ±A/√2 ≈ ±10 cm.
For the same mass on two identical springs in series or parallel, the ratio T_series / T_parallel is:
k_series = k/2, k_parallel = 2k and T ∝ 1/√k. Hence T_series/T_parallel = 2.
The mechanical energy of an ideal linear harmonic oscillator is:
Constant: E = ½kA², while kinetic and potential energies vary
E = Ec + Ep = ½kA² = ½mω²A² = ½mv_max². Potential energy is largest at turning points; kinetic energy is largest at equilibrium.
One A tuning fork has frequency 440 Hz. A second has twice its period. What is its frequency and pitch?
ν = 1/T, so doubling T gives ν = 220 Hz. A 2:1 frequency ratio is one octave. The very-low-frequency phasor sound is only a teaching representation.
